Atiqul Huque Chowdhury ------ Petitioner
vs.
Shahana Rahim and another ------ Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
8. Before this Court the petitioner did not challenge the amount of maintenance or the guardianship of plaintiff No. 2. The only ground urged before us is that the learned lower appellate Court was wrong in giving full dower to the plaintiff No. 1 as the same has already been paid; and if not paid, it is now not payable due to the time bar. However the full payment of dower has not been substantiated as there is nothing in the Kabinnama to show that the ornaments given to the opposite party at the time of the wedding should be considered as 'Usul' and further no evidence has been adduced to prove that Taka 50,000.00 has been paid to the opposite party as the payment of the rest of the dower. 

 10. On the question of limitation he argues that the Family Courts Ordinance is a special law which prescribes no time within which the suit for dower should be filed. In the absence of such a provision he argues that Articles 103 and 104 of the Limitation Act, as the case may be, will apply. In this connection he also refers to section 292 as quoted in Mullah's "Principles of Mohammadan Law" 7th eddition, page 281, according to which in case of a suit for dower, whether prompt or deferred, Articles 103 and 104 will apply respectively and the limitation period will be three years. 

 11. Article 103 of the schedule to the Limitation Act provides: 

 "103. A suit by a Mohammedan for exigible dower shall be instituted within three years from the date when the dower is demanded and refused, or (where during the continuance of the marriage, no such demand has been made) when the marriage is dissolved by death or divorce." 

 14. He further submits that section 20 of the said Ordinance further provides for the application and non-application of certain laws, as for example, the Evidence Act, 1872 and the Code of Civil Procedure, except sections 10 and 11, are made non-applicable to the proceedings before the Family Court; whereas the whole of the Oaths Act is made applicable. At the same time the Ordinance is silent about the application of the Limitation Act. Nothing is said about its applicability to a suit for dower. If it was intended to be applicable it would have been made applicable specifically as has been done in the case of the other Acts. According to him, the sections stated above, namely sections 3 and 20 of the Family Courts Ordinance, 1985, should be read together to come to the conclusion that the Limitation Act is not applicable in a case of a suit for dower. Therefore, any attempt to restrict the limitation period to three years in accordance with Articles 103 and 104 of the Limitation Act will be wrong and beyond the intention of the legislatures. But he was unable to suggest what would then be the limitation period for a suit for dower. 

 17. The Family Court Ordinance is, no doubt, a special law enacted for the special purpose of protecting the interest of the married woman by providing speedy relief. The question then arises, whether it is a self-contained one as suggested by Mr. Hannan. If this is so, and if it prescribed a period of limitation within which a suit for dower should be filed, then section 29(2) of the Limitation Act will apply. A closer scrutiny of the Ordinance shows that no such period has been prescribed in it. Therefore section 29(2) of the Limitation Act is not attracted thus allowing the application of Articles 103 and 104 or any other Article of the Limitation Act. 

 18. From the Kabinnama (Ext. 2) it appears that the dower was fixed at Taka 70,001.00 half of which is prompt and another half is deferred. Article 103 deals with the prompt dower and article 104 deals with the deferred dower. The two articles have already been quoted above. 

 19. Therefore, if there is no demand and a refusal for the prompt dower during the continuance of the marriage the period of limitation under Article 103 would run from the date of the dissolution of the marriage either by death or divorce. In the instant case no demand for prompt dower was made during the continuation of marriage but the demand was made after the marriage was dissolved by divorce, the date of which is 15.4.84, and this is not disputed. So, according to Mr. Das, for that part of dower which is prompt, the period of 3 years will start from the date of divorce i.e. 15.4.84. Similarly, under Article 104 the three years period of limitation for deferred dower would run from the date of dissolution of marriage by death or divorce. However in case of dissolution by divorce the time will start running only when it comes to the notice of the wife. In the instant case there is no dispute as to the date of divorce, so again the limitation period of 3 years for the deferred dower will run from the date of divorce. Therefore it appears that the limitation period for both the prompt and the deferred dowers as provided under Articles 103 and 104 has expired prior to the institution of the suit. Thus Mr. Das submits that the suit is barred by limitation. 

 22. We have already stated that a muslim marriage is contractual in nature, the Kabinnama being the contract with all the terms of the marriage, including the dower and the nature of the dower, laid down in it. Under the Islamic law the dower, prompt or deferred, is no doubt a debt, always due and payable on demand. Therefore, with the demand and refusal to pay it or with the dissolution of marriage by divorce or death, as the case may be, the cause of action would accrue and the statutory period of limitation would begin to run. The question in the instant case is as to how long it would run to complete the period of limitation-will jt be six years under Article 116 or three years under Article 103 and Article 104 of the Limitation Act. 

 36. To sum up, the suit for dower is more or less a suit to enforce a simple money claim founded solely on a contract entered into by the husband, with the wife. The limitation period of the suit depends on when the marriage was entered into with respect to the enactment of the Muslim Marriages and Divorces (Registration) Act, 1974. Marriages taking place after this Act must be registered with the Nikah registrar, according to the Act. Thus in the absence of a prescribed period for a suit for dower Article 116 of the Limitation Act will be applied in preference to Article 103 or 104 of the Limitation Act and the period of limitation will be 6 years.
